However, Aznar government was controversial for some policies: hard line with ETA (refusing negotiations), tensions with Basque and Catalan nationalists, and most controversially, supporting US 2003 Iraq invasion despite majority public opposition. This decision deeply divided Spanish society and would have electoral consequences after Madrid train bombings. PP also faced corruption scandal accusations, though most serious cases wouldn't emerge until later.

events.title: Madrid Train Bombings
events.description: Islamic terrorists linked to Al-Qaeda detonated ten bombs on Madrid commuter trains, killing 193 and wounding over 2,000. This was Spain's deadliest terrorist attack and Europe's worst attack after 9/11. Bombings occurred three days before elections. Aznar government initially blamed ETA, despite evidence quickly pointing to Islamic terrorism, leading to accusations of manipulating information for political gain (ETA attack might rally voters supporting government, while Al-Qaeda attack would focus on unpopular Iraq war policy). Public anger over government handling led to Socialist unexpected victory on March 14. New PM José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero immediately withdrew troops from Iraq. Madrid bombings profoundly impacted Spanish psyche, raising awareness of Islamic terrorism threat and marking major political landscape turning point.

events.title: Economic Crisis and Austerity
events.description: Global financial crisis hit Spain hard, exposing its economy's structural weaknesses, particularly overdependence on construction and real estate bubble. Construction boom collapsed, banks fell into trouble, unemployment soared to 27% (youth unemployment over 50%). Spain faced sovereign debt crisis, forced to implement harsh austerity measures in exchange for EU support. Zapatero's Socialist government implemented cuts in public spending, tax increases, and labor reforms, but lost 2011 elections. New PP government under Mariano Rajoy implemented harsher austerity. Crisis had devastating social impact: massive unemployment, increased poverty, youth emigration, foreclosures, and welfare cuts. It also triggered political upheaval: 2011 May 15 Movement (Indignados) protests occupied squares, emergence of new left-wing party Podemos and centrist Ciudadanos challenging two-party system, acceleration of Catalan independence movement. Crisis undermined trust in traditional parties and institutions, exposed widespread corruption, and reshaped Spanish politics.

events.title: Felipe VI Accession
events.description: Juan Carlos I abdicated after scandals and health problems, his son Prince Felipe becoming Felipe VI. Juan Carlos, once widely respected for his role in democratic transition, saw popularity decline in recent years due to personal scandals (2012 Botswana hunting trip), daughter and son-in-law's corruption cases, and questioning of monarchy's relevance, particularly amid economic crisis and growing republican sentiment. Felipe VI ascended promising to serve 'a new generation of Spaniards' and restore monarchy's prestige. He adopted a more cautious and institutionalized approach, emphasizing transparency and citizen connection. However, he faces major challenges: Catalan independence movement, Juan Carlos's continuing scandals (in 2020 he fled Spain due to financial impropriety), and questioning of monarchy itself, particularly among left and regional nationalists.

events.title: Catalan Independence Referendum Crisis
events.description: Catalan government organized independence referendum despite Spanish Constitutional Court ruling it illegal. Spanish government sent police to stop voting, leading to violent clashes with voters, hundreds injured, scenes broadcast globally. Referendum proceeded chaotically, with Catalan government claiming 90% voted for independence, but turnout only 43%, many unionists boycotting the flawed vote. On October 27, Catalan parliament unilaterally declared independence, Spanish government responded with unprecedented action, invoking Constitution Article 155 to take over Catalonia, dissolve parliament, dismiss President Carles Puigdemont and his government. Puigdemont fled to Belgium, other leaders arrested facing rebellion charges. New regional elections held in December, with pro-independence parties again gaining majority seats, but crisis exposed Catalan society's deep divisions. This was Spain's most serious political crisis since democratic transition, highlighting persistent tensions between central government and Catalonia, between independentists and unionists.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
events.description: Spain became one of Europe's earliest and hardest-hit countries by COVID-19 pandemic. In March 2020, government declared state of emergency, implementing one of Europe's strictest lockdowns, with citizens confined to homes for weeks. Pandemic caused over 120,000 deaths, Spain's per capita death rate among world's highest. Pandemic overwhelmed health systems, particularly in Madrid and Catalonia. Economic impact was catastrophic: GDP fell 11%, tourism collapsed, unemployment soared. Socialist Workers' Party-United Left coalition government under Pedro Sánchez implemented massive fiscal stimulus and European support (particularly EU Recovery Fund). Pandemic also intensified political polarization, with right and left parties fiercely debating government pandemic handling, regional coordination (particularly conflicts with Madrid region), and restriction measures. Pandemic profoundly impacted Spanish society, changing work patterns, urban living, and public health perceptions, while exposing healthcare system and nursing home weaknesses.

events.title: Contemporary Spain: Challenges and Identity
events.description: Spain in 2024 is a complex, democratic, prosperous nation, but facing significant challenges. Politically, the country is EU's fourth-largest economy and stable parliamentary monarchy, but recent years have seen increased political polarization, far-right Vox party's rise, and parliamentary fragmentation making stable government formation difficult. Catalan question remains unresolved: though tensions eased and independence movement leaders pardoned, fundamental divide between independentists and unionists persists. Economically, Spain recovered from COVID crisis but faces high unemployment (particularly youth unemployment), inequality, tourism dependence, and precarious employment. Socially, Spain has become progressive European society, leading in LGBTQ+ rights, gender equality, and secularism, but rural depopulation, aging society, and immigration integration are challenges. Climate change impacts Spain, including droughts, heat waves, and desertification. Culturally, Spain's linguistic and regional diversity is both wealth and tension source. Historical memory remains controversial: debate over Franco legacy handling continues, with 2019 Franco exhumation from Valley of the Fallen triggering fierce debate. Despite challenges, Spain remains vibrant democracy, cultural powerhouse, and important European player, with rich history and diverse identity continuing to shape its 21st-century path.
